Taovaya

Taovaya, also recorded under spellings such as Tawehash, names a particular historical Wichita-related people. Jelks’s focused entry and the Wichita and Affiliated Tribes’ connected history provide a bounded introduction to Red River communities, agriculture, exchange and diplomacy. Historical relationships do not make Taovaya an interchangeable label for every affiliated people or a separate current government here.

Read the sources [1] Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas Online [2] Wichita and Affiliated Tribes; exhibit collaboration credited to the Stovall Museum of Science and History and Oklahoma Archaeological Survey

01

Red River communities and diplomacy

Jelks places Taovaya people in an eighteenth-century movement into southern Oklahoma and northern Texas and describes a settlement near present Spanish Fort by 1759. His account connects the community with the 1758 attack on San Sabá and the successful defense against a Spanish retaliatory expedition in 1759. These episodes are presented as the author’s synthesis, not as a new reading of the expedition papers. The modern place-name Spanish Fort should not turn the Taovaya settlement into a Spanish-built village.

Read the sources [1] Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas Online

02

Farming, exchange and related historical interpretation

The entry describes cultivated crops, seasonal bison hunting and regional exchange, drawing attention to a farming community rather than reducing its history to warfare. The Tribe’s own narrative explicitly includes Taovaya among named peoples. The accompanying Catlin painting is carefully labeled related Wichita grass-lodge context: the museum identifies its subject as Wichita, not Taovaya. It is an outside artist’s nineteenth-century representation and does not identify the pictured individuals or prove that this particular lodge belonged to a Taovaya family.

Read the sources [1] Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas Online [2] Wichita and Affiliated Tribes; exhibit collaboration credited to the Stovall Museum of Science and History and Oklahoma Archaeological Survey

Taovaya Indians ↗

Publication: Originally 1952; revised April 27, 2019

Edward B. Jelks’s focused article identifies Taovaya name variants, a Red River settlement near present Spanish Fort, agriculture, regional exchange and Spanish relations. Historical interpretations remain attributed; its brief treaty/outcome conclusion is not adopted as verified implementation or present status.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Complete main body, web lines 7–11, author, bibliography and publication/revision metadata read. The Bolton and Hodge works, original treaty and underlying encounter records remain unread. Historical labels and the word descendants are not individual genealogy evidence.

Review recorded: October 27, 2026

Access note: Actual public HTML body readable without an account in this inspection. Linked bibliography, archival instruments and media remain separate works unless expressly listed.

https://www.tshaonline.org/handbook/entries/taovaya-indians

Wichita Memories — four connected institutional history chapters ↗

Four linked chapters explain the Tribe’s historical account from early encounters through village life, displacement and continuing community. The credits identify a cooperative exhibit. Treat the chapters as one work, keep named historical groups distinct, and attribute archaeological, treaty and continuity interpretations rather than turning the narrative into independently checked archival evidence.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Complete main narratives of In the Beginning:1540–1750 (lines27–38), People of the Grass House:1750–1820 (27–39), Days of Darkness:1820–1934 (27–37), and A New Beginning:1934–Present (27–38), plus References and Contributors (27–91). Public narrative passages read; no quoted origin stories, ceremonial details, images or underlying bibliography reproduced or separately researched.

Review recorded: October 26, 2026

Access note: Public readable English HTML, no account/paywall encountered. Individual publication/revision dates are unstated; date ranges in titles are historical coverage, not publication dates. Do not repeat historical population estimates as current figures, infer present identities from archaeological phases, or treat institutional treaty summaries as direct readings of the instruments.
